hops.afterHeading: Which neurons die: three diseases, three populations
hops.title: Your big toe versus your eyes in ALS
hops.text: Look from one end of this line to the other, then wiggle your big toe. Both moves ended at lower motor neurons, of very different kinds. Motor neurons in your lower spinal cord send long axons all the way down your leg to the muscles that move your toe. The cells steering your eyes sit in the brainstem, in the oculomotor, trochlear and abducens nuclei, and their short axons reach the eye muscles. In ALS, spinal motor neurons and those that drive speech fail, while the eye-movement neurons hold out late into the disease. That is why patients who can no longer speak can still communicate with eye-tracking computers.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A student sitting cross-legged on a sofa reading a book, glancing sideways while wiggling one big toe in a striped sock.
image.caption: Eye-movement motor neurons tend to resist ALS, so eye tracking can help patients keep communicating.

hops.afterHeading: What builds up: proteins that clump
hops.title: Hibernating ground squirrels phosphorylate tau, then reverse it
hops.text: In deep hibernation, Arctic ground squirrels let their body temperature fall to about zero degrees Celsius, and Syrian hamsters in torpor cool to about five. Torpor comes in bouts lasting days, broken by brief rewarmings. During each bout, tau in their neurons picks up extra phosphate groups, the same kind of change found in Alzheimer tangles. In European ground squirrels, phosphorylated tau stains most strongly in the ventral hippocampus, entorhinal cortex and isocortex, while synaptic contacts onto CA3 neurons recede. Researchers found no tau filaments in the tissue they examined. Within hours of rewarming, tau phosphorylation falls and markers of those CA3 synapses begin to recover.

sources.citation: Arendt et al., Journal of Neuroscience 23(18):6972-6981 (2003).

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A ground squirrel curled asleep in a grass-lined burrow beneath a snowy winter surface.
image.caption: In hibernating ground squirrels, tau gains phosphates during torpor and starts losing them as the animals warm up.

hops.afterHeading: What can start it: genes that cause and genes that raise risk
hops.title: An Alzheimer risk allele linked to better scores in older Tsimane with high eosinophil counts
hops.text: APOE ε4 is often described as if carrying it sealed a person's fate. It raises the odds of late-onset Alzheimer disease, yet its link to thinking can change with conditions. A study of 372 Tsimane forager-horticulturalists in the Bolivian Amazon asked how APOE ε4 and blood eosinophil counts, an indirect marker of parasitic infection, together relate to cognitive test scores. Among participants aged 45 to 88 with high eosinophil counts, ε4 carriers tended to score higher than non-carriers, whereas at lower counts they scored worse. The authors hypothesize that ε4 may carry an advantage in high-pathogen settings that fades with lower infection exposure.

sources.citation: Trumble et al., The FASEB Journal 31(4):1508-1515 (2017).

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A wooden dugout canoe and woven baskets of plantains along a lush sunlit riverbank in the Amazon rainforest.
image.caption: At high blood eosinophil counts, a parasite marker, older Tsimane APOE ε4 carriers tended to score higher than non-carriers.
